legend: Dorsopalmar radiograph of the left hand. Multiple enchondromas are seen in the metacarpals and phalanges. There is faint internal density in several of the tumours, but punctate matrix mineralization is inconspicuous. Expansile lesions in the proximal phalanges of the index and little fingers are consistent with subperiosteal chondromas (likely to have commenced within the cortex or deep to periosteum) and show mild diffuse density, with small punctate foci of calcification in the little finger lesion. Growth disturbance of the ulna causes mild shortening.

Coronal short-tau inversion recovery (STIR) MRI of the left hand shows multiple enchondromas. Metacarpal tumours are central medullary lesions; both medullary and subperiosteal/intracortical lesions are seen in the phalanges. The tumours are lobular, and they show marked hyperintensity and thin, low-signal septations. There is marked expansile remodelling of the lesions in the proximal phalanges of the index and little finger.
Multiple enchondromas are present in the metatarsal bones and phalanges.
Multiple cartilaginous nodules separated by bone marrow and encased by cancellous bone (a sign of slow growth). Host bone permeation is never seen in enchondromas.

The chondrocytes are embedded within a hyaline matrix, with the typical finely stippled calcification. Tumour cells are located within large lacunae, in which the cytoplasm is pushed aside, forming spider-like extensions. The nuclei are small and hyperchromatic, with no visible nucleoli.
Endochondral calcification is a characteristic feature. Note the necrotic chondrocytes.
Spindle cell and cavernous haemangioma containing multiple phleboliths within dilated vessels.
